jurisdiction.name: Thailand
local_terms: หนูท้องขาว

summary: Thailand is permissive by default for the roof rat. The Wild Animal Conservation and Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019) regulates only species on its conserved/protected/controlled schedules, and R. rattus is on none of them. Thai law treats it 'functionally rather than nominally': it doesn't name 'domesticated rats' as exempt; rather, an unscheduled species simply falls outside the Department of National Parks (DNP) wildlife-permit system, so you never have to prove a roof rat is captive-bred vs. wild-caught. R. rattus is classified as a native/naturalized 'Least Concern' agricultural pest, pointedly NOT an Invasive Alien Species (that label, and its management mandates, fall on R. norvegicus), so there is no eradication/possession ban aimed at pet keepers. Keeping/breeding/giving a captive-bred roof rat is therefore unregulated at the federal level, subject only to the Cruelty Prevention & Welfare of Animals Act B.E. 2557 (2014) care duties; small rodents are sold openly (e.g., Chatuchak market). Bangkok's Animal Keeping Ordinance B.E. 2567 (2024) adds property-size pet-density quotas that textually include 'mammals' (so they could touch caged rats), but its registration/microchipping mandate is limited to dogs and cats, enforcement is nuisance-complaint driven, and the council DELAYED the whole ordinance one year, now effective 10 January 2027. The one hard permit step is IMPORT: bringing a live rodent into Thailand requires a Department of Livestock Development (DLD) import permit (Form R1/1), an origin-authority-endorsed veterinary health certificate, a 500 THB/animal fee, and a discretionary (often-waived) 30-day quarantine. Internal inter-province movement technically falls under the Animal Epidemics Act B.E. 2558 (2015) R-form chain, but that targets livestock and is not enforced against private pet rodents. No Thai law expressly prohibits private keeping/breeding/transfer of captive-bred R. rattus. Never release a nonnative.

keep.why: R. rattus is absent from every DNP conserved/protected/controlled wildlife schedule under WACPA B.E. 2562 (which regulates only scheduled species), so DNP wildlife jurisdiction simply does not attach, and because the test is scheduling, not 'domestication,' there is no requirement to prove a kept rat is captive-bred. It is classified as a native/naturalized 'Least Concern' agricultural pest, NOT an Invasive Alien Species (that designation falls on R. norvegicus under ONEP's IAS List 1), so no possession/eradication mandate targets private keepers. The Cruelty Prevention & Welfare of Animals Act B.E. 2557 (2014) imposes baseline care duties on any kept animal but bans no non-listed species. Bangkok's B.E. 2567 (2024) ordinance designates 'mammals' a controlled category with property-size density quotas (so it textually could reach caged rats), but registration/microchipping is dog/cat-only, enforcement is nuisance-driven, and the ordinance is delayed to 10 Jan 2027. 'Unclear' only because no official text affirmatively names R. rattus as a permitted pet; legality is derived from its absence on all prohibited schedules.
keep.governing_law: Wild Animal Conservation & Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019) (scheduled species only); Cruelty Prevention & Welfare of Animals Act B.E. 2557 (2014); Bangkok Animal Keeping Ordinance B.E. 2567 (2024) (delayed to 10 Jan 2027).

breed.why: Breeding a non-scheduled, non-CITES species is outside the WACPA permit system, and there is no DNP/DLD 'rat-breeder licence' for domestic non-livestock rodents. Private, non-commercial breeding, keeping or giving away offspring, is entirely unregulated beyond welfare duties; small rodents are bred and sold openly (Chatuchak). The regulated layer attaches to the PREMISES and OPERATOR, not the species: under the Public Health Act B.E. 2535 (1992), local municipalities classify commercial animal breeding/boarding/retail as a 'hazardous activity to health' (กิจการที่เป็นอันตรายต่อสุขภาพ) needing a district-office premises permit (waste/ventilation/zoning inspection). Thai law sets no codified numeric threshold where a hobbyist becomes 'commercial,' so occasional give-away or cost-covering breeding is, in practice, ignored until scale generates waste/traffic/nuisance.
breed.governing_law: WACPA B.E. 2562 (controlled-wildlife breeding permit, N/A to unlisted); Public Health Act B.E. 2535 (1992) (municipal 'hazardous activity' premises permit at commercial scale).

sell_give.why: Trade restrictions under WACPA apply only to scheduled/controlled wildlife, so no wildlife statute bars selling or gifting a captive-bred R. rattus, and non-commercial gifting between private parties is unrestricted (beyond welfare duties). Operating as a retail business adds general Department of Business Development (DBD) registration plus, at premises scale, the same municipal 'hazardous activity to health' permit as breeding, these attach to the business/premises, not to the species. Not CITES-listed. Ambiguity remains only over whether open-market sale of unlisted rodents needs a specific DLD animal-dealer licence or merely a local commercial-premises permit (the DR found the latter to be the practical answer).
sell_give.governing_law: WACPA B.E. 2562 (scheduled species only); DBD business registration + Public Health Act B.E. 2535 (commercial premises); not CITES-listed.

transport.why: Regardless of its unlisted wildlife status, the Department of Livestock Development (DLD) holds absolute authority over the movement of all live animals under the Animal Epidemics Act B.E. 2558 (2015); for cross-border movement R. rattus is treated as a 'restricted live animal.' IMPORT requires: (1) an advance DLD import permit (Form R1/1), applied for at the Animal Quarantine Station at the port of entry no fewer than 7 and no more than 60 days before travel; (2) an Official Health Certificate from an accredited origin-country vet within 10 days of travel, formally endorsed (wet-ink) by the origin national veterinary authority (e.g., USDA APHIS), electronic copies are routinely rejected; (3) a 500 THB/animal fee at the airport, after which the officer issues the Notice of Import Approval (R-6) and Import Licence (R-7). The DLD holds discretionary authority to impose a 30-day quarantine on imported rodents but frequently waives it for healthy private pets with flawless paperwork from low-risk origins. Microchipping is strictly mandated for dogs/cats and only ambiguously for rodents, strongly advised (or get written AQS confirmation that photographic ID suffices). INTERNAL inter-province movement technically falls under the Animal Epidemics Act R.3/R.4 movement-permit chain, but that text targets agricultural livestock and is not enforced against private pet rats (negligible-enforcement gray zone). Never release a nonnative.
transport.governing_law: Animal Epidemics Act B.E. 2558 (2015); DLD import permit (Form R1/1) + Official Health Certificate + R-6/R-7; discretionary 30-day quarantine.

restrictions.summary: Keeping/breeding/giving a captive-bred roof rat in Thailand needs no wildlife permit (R. rattus is unscheduled), only welfare-law care. The one hard permit step is IMPORT: a DLD import permit (Form R1/1, applied for 7-60 days ahead at the port-of-entry Animal Quarantine Station) + an origin-authority-endorsed veterinary health certificate (issued within 10 days, wet-ink) + a 500 THB/animal fee, with a discretionary (often-waived) 30-day quarantine. Microchipping is advised for rodents (mandatory for dogs/cats; ambiguous for rats, confirm with the AQS).
steps: Apply for the DLD import permit (Form R1/1) at the destination Animal Quarantine Station 7-60 days before travel
Obtain an Official Health Certificate from an accredited origin-country vet within 10 days, endorsed (wet-ink) by the origin national authority (e.g., USDA APHIS)
On arrival use the 'Goods to Declare' channel; pay 500 THB/animal; receive the R-6 (approval) and R-7 (import licence)
Microchip the rat if biologically safe, or get written AQS confirmation that photographic ID is accepted

forms.name: DLD Import Permit (Form R1/1), Animal Quarantine Station

restrictions.where_to_file: Department of Livestock Development (DLD), Animal Quarantine Station (port of entry, e.g. Suvarnabhumi)
restrictions.fees: 500 THB per animal (airport processing); origin-country vet fee for the health certificate

restrictions.summary: Bangkok only: the Animal Keeping Ordinance B.E. 2567 (2024) sets property-size pet-density quotas (e.g., 1 pet in a 20-80 sq.m condo; up to 2 over 80 sq.m) for 'controlled' categories that textually include 'mammals,' so several caged rats could in principle count toward the limit. Registration/microchipping under the ordinance applies to dogs and cats only, and enforcement is nuisance-complaint driven, keep enclosures clean, secure, and odor-free. The ordinance's effective date was postponed one year to 10 January 2027. Commercial breeding/retail premises separately need a municipal 'hazardous activity to health' permit under the Public Health Act B.E. 2535.
steps: In Bangkok, keep rat enclosures secure, ventilated, and sanitary to avoid nuisance complaints (the practical enforcement trigger)
If breeding/selling at commercial scale, obtain the district-office 'hazardous activity to health' premises permit
restrictions.where_to_file: Bangkok Metropolitan Administration district office (Veterinary Public Health) / your local municipality

restrictions.summary: It is illegal to release/abandon any captive animal into the public domain under Thai urban animal-abandonment ordinances, and R. rattus is a documented agricultural pest, keep them contained and rehome responsibly; never release.

inquiry_focus: (1) DNP: written confirmation that Rattus rattus (หนูดำ/หนูท้องขาว) is unlisted under every ministerial schedule (conserved/protected/controlled) of the Wild Animal Conservation & Protection Act B.E. 2562, so a private hobbyist needs no possession/breeding/trade permit. (2) DLD AQS: full documentation to import a captive-bred pet R. rattus (Form R1/1 + USDA-endorsed Official Health Certificate), is an ISO microchip strictly mandated for small rodents or is photographic ID a legal substitute, and does inter-province domestic transport of a pet rat require an R.3 movement permit? (3) BMA: do the B.E. 2567 condo pet-density limits apply to small caged mammals like pet rats, and at what threshold does home breeding of R. rattus require a municipal 'hazardous activity to health' premises permit?
